245: (1) A Jew and a non-Jew, etc.— Know that it is entirely permitted if the Jew has some business or labor in partnership with the non-Jew, and they stipulate from the outset, before entering the partnership: “Work now on Shabbat and take according to your labor, whether much or little, and I will work one weekday in exchange and take according to my labor.” At the time of profit division, the non-Jew takes the earnings for Shabbat, and the Jew takes for the weekday in exchange, whether much or little. But if they did not stipulate from the beginning, and at the time of division the Jew says to the non-Jew, “You take for your labor on Shabbat and I for mine on the weekday,” this is certainly forbidden. And if they did not stipulate from the outset and at the time of division they simply divided equally, this is a question in the Talmud and unresolved. The Rambam ruled stringently, and the Rosh leniently. The Shulchan Aruch ruled like the Rambam, and the Rema ruled in his gloss like the Rosh in cases of significant financial loss. But if they stipulated before entering the partnership as described above, and at the time of division they agreed to divide equally, this is permitted even according to the Rambam, as written in section 2. These are the main rulings of the opening paragraphs, and the rest of the details and their reasoning will be explained later. A field or an oven, etc. — The reason for these rulings requiring a stipulation is that otherwise, at the time the partnership was formed, the labor was imposed on both of them jointly. Therefore, if afterward the Jew says to the non-Jew, “You work alone on Shabbat and take all the profit of Shabbat, and I will work alone one weekday in exchange and take that day’s profit for myself,” it is as if he appoints the non-Jew as a laborer with his own hands, as if saying, “You work for me on Shabbat, and I will work for you on a weekday,” and he becomes his agent in full [Tosafot]. Accordingly, if the non-Jewish partner himself does nothing, but other non-Jews who come to bake fire up the jointly owned oven and pay some fee for its use, the Jew may receive from his partner the portion of the profit due to him according to his share, even if they did not stipulate—provided he does not take payment solely for Shabbat, but rather receives it as a general payment blended with other days, so that it is not considered Shabbat wages. And we are not concerned about the appearance that people might say the non-Jew is doing it for the Jew, since it is known that the non-Jew has a share in it [Magen Avraham and Sha’ar HaTziyun].
